title: When forecasters agree on the size and not on the growth
excerpt: We reported that published estimates disagree about size far more than about growth. Two of five markets sized this week invert that. The ratio between the two spreads diagnoses which disagreement you have — and each needs a different fix.
author: NeoGraph Analytics Research Desk
content:
In Why two forecasts of the same market differ by ten times we reported a pattern from ten markets: published estimates of a market's current size disagree enormously, by up to 24x, while the growth rates those same publishers attach to it barely disagree at all. We drew the obvious conclusion. A spread that wide is a labelling failure, not an analytical one, and the fix is to name the scope you mean.

Five markets sized this week say that conclusion was too general. Two of them disagree about growth more than they disagree about size — the exact inverse — and in those two the fix we recommended does nothing at all, because the publishers already agree what the market is.

The two spreads, side by side

Each figure below is measured the same way. Every published estimate for the market is normalised to a 2026 base year at its own publisher's stated growth rate before any comparison, so the size spread is like-for-like and not an artefact of different base years. The CAGR spread is the ratio of the highest published rate to the lowest. The last column is simply the first divided by the second.

MarketSize spreadCAGR spreadRatio
Dialysis and renal care6.65x1.80x3.7
Ambulatory surgery centres3.47x2.23x1.6
Contract research organisations2.06x1.38x1.5
Radiotherapy equipment1.39x1.50x0.9
Pharmacovigilance1.50x2.92x0.5

The ratio sorts these five into two genuinely different problems, and a reader who treats them the same will misread three of the five.

A ratio above two is a scope problem

Dialysis is the clean case, and the most extreme we have measured. Its published 2026 estimates run from $20.29B to roughly $134.90B. That is not a range of opinions; it is four distinct markets sharing one name. Machines as a capital good at $20.29B. Machines plus dialysers, bloodlines and concentrates at $30.01B. The clinic business that actually performs the treatment at $83.97B. All of that plus dialysis drugs at $130-135B. Meanwhile the growth rates sit in a 4.60% to 8.30% band — the publishers broadly concur on how fast dialysis grows and disagree by a factor of six-and-a-half about what dialysis is.

You can settle an argument like that with arithmetic, because the tiers make different claims about who earns the money. Fresenius Medical Care booked EUR 19,628M in FY2025 and DaVita $13.643B; converted at the ECB's 2025 annual average, that is $35.82B between two companies. Two firms out-earning the entire published machines market by 1.77x settles whether the machines figure can be quoted as the market. It cannot.

Ambulatory surgery centres sit lower on the ratio but carry the most flagrant version of the same failure. One publisher's figure for the United States and Europe, $124.04B, exceeds four other publishers' global figures. Another publisher's US-only figure of $48.75B exceeds a third publisher's entire global market of $47.68B. And one house sizes the "global ambulatory surgical centers market" at $4.76B while listing GE, Philips and Getinge as its key players — an equipment slice published under a facility-market name. No amount of care about growth rates helps a reader who has picked up the wrong one of those.

A ratio below one is a forecasting problem, and it does not yield to scope discipline

Pharmacovigilance is where our earlier conclusion breaks. Its eight whole-function estimates for 2026 span only 1.50x — $9.14B to $13.71B — which is tighter agreement about size than almost any market we have sized. Its growth rates span 2.92x, from 5.6% to 16.34%. By 2032 those rates have pulled the endpoints 2.68x apart, from $12.76B to $34.17B.

There is a reason the sizes agree. Pharmacovigilance is statutorily defined. Marketing authorisation holders must collect, assess and report adverse events; the obligation is written into law in every major jurisdiction, so every publisher is counting the same work. There is no scope lever to pull and no tier to name. What they are disagreeing about is whether that obligation gets heavier, and by how much.

Which is checkable, because the obligation has a counter. FDA's FAERS received 1,307,769 reports in 2025, 16.5% below its 2021 peak of 1,566,148. EudraVigilance processed 1,765,581 individual case safety reports in 2025, 7.5% below 2023. Intake is flat to falling. Hold it constant and the published forecast implies the dollars of pharmacovigilance spend per adverse-event report received rise from $7,991 in 2026 to $15,586 in 2032. Every CAGR in that market is a forecast of regulatory intensity per case, and no publisher says so.

Radiotherapy equipment lands at 0.9 for a structurally similar reason. The installed fleet is a public register — the IAEA's DIRAC directory counts roughly 17,000 teletherapy units across about 8,700 centres — and the supply side is three companies. When the denominator is counted and the vendors are few, there is very little room to disagree about size: strip out two estimates that fail their own internal arithmetic and the remaining ten span 1.39x. What is genuinely unknown is the replacement cycle. $8,140M over 17,000 units is $478,824 per unit per year, and whether that is the right number depends entirely on whether a linac is replaced on a ten-year or a fifteen-year rhythm. That is a real uncertainty about the future, not a confusion about the present.

Two forecasts already contradict their own volume registers

The useful consequence of separating the two problems is that growth disagreements can be tested against counts, where scope disagreements cannot.

Contract research is the sharpest case. Its published forecast is 8.90% a year. Industry-led interventional trial starts registered on ClinicalTrials.gov ran 6,399, 6,044, 5,726, 5,600 and 5,904 across 2021 to 2025 — a compound decline of 1.99%, and 12.5% below peak at the trough. The aggregate of eight disclosed CRO revenue lines grew 3.13% in 2025, and a single mid-size firm supplied 37.8% of that growth from 6.9% of the base. So the published rate is roughly 2.8x the measured one on a volume base that is not growing. That can still be right — price and trial complexity can carry revenue while trial counts fall — but it is a claim about price per trial, and it should be stated as one.

Ambulatory surgery centres can be decomposed the same way, and the decomposition is unusually clean. MedPAC publishes the components of its own 2024 increase, and multiplying them back — 1.032 x 1.008 x 1.084 x 1.004 — reproduces its published 13.0% rise to within 0.2 points. Of the 13.2 points, 8.4 are case mix and 0.8 is volume. The migration of procedures out of hospitals into ambulatory centres is doing almost all the work, and migration has an endpoint. That is why we publish the conservative 4.40% rate for that market rather than the 9.80% also available in the literature.

How to use the ratio

Compute both spreads before you choose a number. Normalise every estimate to one base year at its own publisher's rate, take the ratio of highest to lowest size, take the ratio of highest to lowest CAGR, and divide.

If the result is above about two, you have a scope problem. Do not average, do not pick a brand: identify the tiers, name the one you mean, and check it against something countable — disclosed revenue of the largest participants, a facility census, a regulated unit price. Three of the four dialysis tiers can be eliminated by arithmetic alone.

If the result is below about one, the publishers already agree what the market is, and averaging their growth rates is averaging their guesses about the future. Find the market's volume counter — adverse-event reports received, trial registrations, installed units, certified facilities — and ask what each candidate rate implies per unit of that volume by the end of the forecast. In pharmacovigilance that question turns a choice between 5.6% and 16.34% into a concrete statement about cost per case, which a reader can actually hold an opinion about.

And if a market's own estimates fail their own arithmetic, say so rather than quietly dropping them. Two of the twelve radiotherapy estimates we collected do: one states a 7.10% CAGR its own endpoints put at 6.43%, and attaches a cardiology, urology, gynaecology and neurology application list to a radiotherapy market; another prints two base years, two end years and a third CAGR on one page. We report the raw 3.38x spread and the 1.39x spread that remains once those two are removed, because which estimates were excluded, and why, is part of the finding.

Sources

Spreads computed from published estimates collected for each report, normalised to a 2026 base at each publisher's own stated CAGR; the full estimate tables, with publisher, publication date, base year and stated scope for every figure, are in the five reports linked above. Volume registers: FDA openFDA drug/event counts by receive date; European Medicines Agency EudraVigilance annual report EMA/371010/2025; ClinicalTrials.gov API v2, industry-led interventional studies by start year; IAEA DIRAC Directory of Radiotherapy Centres; MedPAC Report to the Congress, ambulatory surgical centre and outpatient dialysis chapters. Company figures: FY2025 filings and results releases of Fresenius Medical Care, DaVita, IQVIA, ICON, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Labcorp, Fortrea, Medpace, Charles River Laboratories, Hangzhou Tigermed, Siemens Healthineers, Elekta and Accuray.
